_meta.description: Curated, cited Apache Iceberg + AWS best-practice knowledge pack for the agentic advisory layer. Each entry: recommendation, the Iceberg property/CALL procedure, a threshold/trigger, and source URLs to cite.
_meta.note: Reconciled with a 5-angle deep-research pass (17 primary sources, 25 claims, all 3-0 adversarially verified vs Apache Iceberg docs / AWS Athena docs / AWS Prescriptive Guidance) on 2026-06-16. The agent retrieves locally (no runtime web egress).
_meta.verification: All defaults/thresholds below were confirmed against primary sources; values track the Iceberg 'latest' branch and AWS docs as of 2026-06-16.

small_files.recommendation: Many small data files inflate metadata and slow scans because every file is an open/plan/read unit. Keep the 512 MB default target file size and compact with the rewrite_data_files action (default 'binpack' strategy), which bin-packs small files into larger ones. By default it selects files smaller than 75% of target (i.e. < 384 MB for a 512 MB target) and rewrites any file group with min-input-files (5) or more files. Trigger compaction when a table (or partition) has many files well below the target, especially from streaming/trickle ingestion. On Athena (engine v3) the equivalent is OPTIMIZE <table> REWRITE DATA USING BIN_PACK.
small_files.procedure: CALL <catalog>.system.rewrite_data_files(table => 'db.tbl', options => map('target-file-size-bytes','536870912','min-input-files','5'))  -- Athena: OPTIMIZE db.tbl REWRITE DATA USING BIN_PACK
small_files.strategy: bin-pack (default) just compacts; use strategy => 'sort' (sort_order => 'col ASC' or 'zorder(c1,c2)') to also cluster data for better file pruning. Selection defaults: MIN_FILE_SIZE_DEFAULT_RATIO=75% of target, MAX=180%, MIN_INPUT_FILES=5; MAX_FILE_GROUP_SIZE_BYTES=100 GB per Spark job (raise for partition-level sort).
small_files.threshold: Compact when avg data-file size is well under the target (e.g. < 32 MB, and certainly anything < 384 MB qualifies for the default ratio) and there are >= 5 files per partition; or when small_files / data_files is a large fraction. Partitions with < 5 files are skipped by default.

compaction_strategy.topic: Choosing a compaction strategy (bin-pack vs sort vs zorder)
compaction_strategy.recommendation: Use bin-pack (default) for the pure small-file problem — it is the cheapest and just packs files to the target size. Use sort when queries filter/aggregate on specific columns and you want data clustered for file pruning. Use zorder when queries filter on multiple columns. Sort/zorder rewrites cost more but improve scan efficiency.
compaction_strategy.property: rewrite_data_files options: strategy => 'sort' | 'binpack'; sort_order => 'col ASC NULLS FIRST'
compaction_strategy.threshold: Match the strategy to query patterns; don't sort/zorder if queries don't filter on the columns.

partitioning.topic: Partition design, transforms, evolution, and skew
partitioning.recommendation: Use Iceberg hidden partitioning with transforms (days/months/years/hours on timestamps, bucket(N) on high-cardinality keys, truncate(N) on strings) rather than raw partition columns — this avoids extra derived columns and lets queries prune without users knowing the partition scheme. Avoid over-partitioning: too many small partitions create many small files and large metadata. Aim for partitions large enough to hold target-size files. Iceberg supports partition evolution (change the spec without rewriting old data) — use it instead of rebuilding the table. For skew (a few hot partition values dominating), consider bucketing the hot dimension or a secondary partition field to spread writes.
partitioning.property: PARTITIONED BY (days(ts)), bucket(16, id), truncate(10, name); partition evolution via ALTER TABLE ... ADD/DROP PARTITION FIELD
partitioning.threshold: AWS rule of thumb: 'too many partitions' = the data size in the MAJORITY of partitions is less than 2-5x write.target-file-size-bytes (i.e. most partitions can't even fill a few target-size files). Also watch for one partition holding a large fraction of rows (skew, e.g. hot_partition_share > 0.4). Fix granularity with partition evolution (e.g. hourly -> daily) rather than rebuilding.

snapshots.recommendation: Every write creates a snapshot. Data files are NOT deleted while still referenced by a retained snapshot usable for time travel/rollback, so unbounded snapshot growth keeps stale files alive and bloats metadata (manifest lists, metadata.json). Run expire_snapshots regularly. Procedure defaults: older_than = 5 days ago, retain_last = 1 (mirroring table properties history.expire.max-snapshot-age-ms=432000000 and history.expire.min-snapshots-to-keep=1). Iceberg classifies expire_snapshots as RECOMMENDED (routine) maintenance. On Athena (engine v3) the equivalent is VACUUM (defaults: vacuum_max_snapshot_age_seconds=432000 / 5 days, vacuum_min_snapshots_to_keep=1).
snapshots.procedure: CALL <catalog>.system.expire_snapshots(table => 'db.tbl', older_than => TIMESTAMP '<cutoff>', retain_last => 5)  -- Athena: VACUUM db.tbl
snapshots.threshold: Expire when snapshot count grows large (tens to hundreds from frequent commits) or older than your retention window. Common cadence: daily/weekly. Tune retain_last / older_than up if you need a longer time-travel window.

orphan_files.recommendation: Failed or aborted writes can leave data/metadata files in storage that no snapshot references (orphans). Run remove_orphan_files periodically to reclaim that storage. Use a conservative older_than (default 3 days) so you don't delete files from in-flight writes.
orphan_files.threshold: Run on a slow cadence (e.g. weekly/monthly); always with a safe older_than to avoid races with running writes. Run AFTER expire_snapshots.

manifests.recommendation: Iceberg plans queries by reading manifest files. Many small manifests (common after frequent commits) slow planning. rewrite_manifests rebuilds them into fewer, better-organized manifests, clustering entries by partition for faster pruning. Note: Iceberg classifies this as OPTIONAL maintenance (a tuning step), not routine — run it when manifest counts are demonstrably hurting query planning, after compaction and snapshot expiry have already reduced manifest churn.
manifests.threshold: Rewrite when there are many manifests with a low average files-per-manifest, or after disabling auto-merge for ingestion. Planning-time symptom: slow query planning on a table with many manifests.

merge_on_read.topic: Merge-on-read vs copy-on-write and delete files
merge_on_read.recommendation: Delete/update/merge default to copy-on-write (CoW) and can be switched to merge-on-read (MoR) — only on format-version 2+ — via write.{delete,update,merge}.mode. CoW rewrites whole data files on each change (fast reads, expensive writes; good for read-heavy tables with infrequent updates). MoR writes delete files (position or equality) instead (fast writes, but reads reconcile deletes, causing read amplification as delete files accumulate). IMPORTANT: ordinary rewrite_data_files does NOT merge delete files into data files unless you set the DELETE_FILE_THRESHOLD option (e.g. '3' = rewrite a data file once 3+ delete files reference it; default is effectively disabled). For minor compaction of just the small delete files, use rewrite_position_delete_files (64 MB target; always filters out dangling deletes). Switch to CoW (or compact more aggressively) if read amplification from accumulating deletes hurts query latency.
merge_on_read.threshold: Address when delete_files / data_files (delete ratio) climbs — a delete ratio above ~0.1 is a good trigger to rewrite. Equality deletes are costlier at read time than position deletes. Remember plain compaction won't clear deletes without delete-file-threshold set.

format_v2.recommendation: Format v2 enables row-level deletes/updates (the delete-file mechanism behind MoR). Use v2 when you need UPDATE/DELETE/MERGE. With v2 comes responsibility for delete-file maintenance (see merge_on_read). Set format-version=2 at create time; most engines (Athena engine v3, Glue/Spark with Iceberg) support v2.
format_v2.threshold: Choose v2 for mutable tables; keep maintenance (compaction, expire, delete rewrite) scheduled.
